title: Is there a Balkan fertility paradox? (from my email) - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: Reader Thomas Hanes documents that the Balkans may be the only region outside central Asia where fertility rose from 2015 to 2026, now holding Europe's top four TFRs (Montenegro 1.8, Bulgaria 1.73, Moldova 1.73, Serbia 1.64, ahead of France at 1.61) after having Europe's lowest rates in the post-Soviet nadir — with no available explanation, since comparable post-communist states show no parallel rise.

insights.claim: The Balkans may be the only region outside central Asia where fertility has increased between 2015 and 2026, making it a genuine outlier against the global fertility decline.
insights.so_what: The only counterexample to a near-universal trend is where the causal mechanism is most likely to be identifiable — worth tracking for pronatalist policy design.
insights.quote: The Balkans may be the only region other than central Asia where fertility has increased from 2015 to 2026.
insights.locator: The Balkans may be the only region
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen

insights.claim: As of 2024 the four highest fertility rates in Europe are Montenegro at 1.8, Bulgaria at 1.73, Moldova at 1.73 and Serbia at 1.64, all ahead of France at 1.61.
insights.so_what: France is the standard reference case for European pronatalism and is now being beaten by countries with far weaker family-policy spending.
insights.quote: Montenegro (1.8), Bulgaria (1.73) Moldova (1.73), and Serbia (1.64) are top four. France was next at 1.61.
insights.locator: All of the highest fertility rates in Europe
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen

insights.claim: The Balkan position is a full reversal: during the post-Soviet nadir the region had perhaps the lowest fertility in Europe, rates rose around 2010, and have continued slowly rising since.
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that collapsed fertility can revert without an obvious policy trigger, which argues against treating low fertility as a one-way ratchet.
insights.quote: During the post-soviet nadir, the Balkans had perhaps the lowest fertility in Europe.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen

insights.claim: Even the lowest Balkan countries — Macedonia, Romania, Albania and Hungary at roughly 1.35 to 1.4 — sit above typical Southern European and former Warsaw Pact/USSR levels despite being lowish by Western European standards.
insights.so_what: The regional floor is elevated, not just the top end, which points to a regional rather than country-specific driver.
insights.quote: The lowest Balkan countries (Macedonia, Romania, Albania, and Hungary) sit at ~1.35-1.4
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen

insights.claim: Culturally and economically similar post-communist states — Ukraine, Belarus, Poland and the Baltics — show no parallel fertility increase, ruling out generic post-communist convergence as the cause.
insights.so_what: The natural control group diverges, which is what makes this a genuine puzzle rather than a regional artifact.
insights.quote: Ostensibly similar cultures/economies have no parallel increase (Ukraine, Belarus, Poland, and the Baltics).
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen

insights.claim: Neither male domestic contribution nor religiosity explains the Balkan result, since Balkan men are reputed to be unhelpful husbands and fathers and the region is no more religious than Poland, Italy or Belarus.
insights.so_what: The two dominant fertility explanations — gender-equitable parenting and religiosity — both fail here, weakening their use as policy levers elsewhere.
insights.quote: Balkan men are famously unhelpful husbands and fathers, and the Balkans aren’t any more religious than Poland, Italy and Belarus.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen

insights.claim: The author explicitly has no theory that fits the pattern and is soliciting one, so the Balkan case should be treated as an open empirical question rather than support for any existing fertility model.
insights.so_what: Guard against anyone claiming the Balkans as evidence for their preferred pronatalist policy — the mechanism is unidentified.
insights.quote: I don’t have any theory that would explain this pattern.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
